proofs.proof_tex:
By the full-observation definition, there is a fixed Borel map \(T_n\) such that \(W_n=T_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Hence every score test \(\psi_n\in\Psi_n\) induces the full-observation test \(\psi_n\circ T_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) with exactly the same rejection probability under every \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  The admissible score tests are therefore a subclass of the admissible full-observation tests, and the two minimax definitions give
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 \ge s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}. \tag{1}
\]
The full-observable minimax theorem then yields, for every \(0<a\le2B\),
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 \ge \frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{2}
\]
That theorem's upper-bound proof uses the unchanged statistic \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), which is itself a common Borel function of the score vector \(W_n\).  Its established uniform size and power therefore also give
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}\le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{3}
\]
The exactly unbiased proposition separately shows that
\(\mathbf 1\{\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}>q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)\}\)
is a common Borel score-vector test with level at most \(\alpha\), power at least \(1-\beta\) when
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)+q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta)\), and no sample-centering bias term.  Finally, choose any fixed \(a\in(0,2B]\).  Since \(N_n=n-2r\), (2) is bounded below by a positive constant times \(n^{-1/2}\); the established formula for \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)\) is \(O(n^{-1/2})\) when \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\) are fixed.  Equations (2)--(3) prove the claimed \(\Theta(n^{-1/2})\) score-vector rate.  The score radius in this statement is, by definition, restricted to common Borel maps of \(W_n\); the separate full-observable theorem supplies the stronger converse for the richer declared observation.

added_lemmas.statement:
In the canonical full-observable experiment, suppose \(e_1\ne e_0\), \(p=1/2\), and \(\alpha+\beta<1\).  For every fixed \(a\) satisfying \(0<a\le2B\) and every integer \(n>4r+1\),
\[
 \frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}
 \le s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 \le \rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
Consequently, for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\) with \(\alpha+\beta<1\) and \(p=1/2\),
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The upper bound is attained by the unchanged sample-mean-centered test \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), viewed as a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The lower bound ranges over every common Borel randomized test of the vector containing the observed graph, assignments, exposures, realized outcomes, and known propensity coordinates.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
We first prove the upper bound.  By the definition of the full observation, \(W_n\) is a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\): each score is obtained from one realized outcome, the two exposure indicators, and the two strictly positive known propensity coordinates.  Hence the statistic \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\), and therefore \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), is a common Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The established size--separation theorem gives, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\alpha
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[1-\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\beta
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
The definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) therefore yields
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{1}
\]

We prove the converse with an exact-local, causal-realizable, common-support submodel.  Fix \(a\in(0,2B]\) and put \(b=a/2\), so \(0<b\le B\).  Let the graph be the deterministic nearest-neighbor line, let \(U_i\) be iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) variables, take
\[
 E_i(d,G)=
 \begin{cases}
 e_1,&d_i=1,\\
 e_0,&d_i=0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 C_i(d)=(d_i,d_{i+1})\in\mathcal C:=\{00,01,10,11\},
\]
and draw the two assignment waves conditionally independently with iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) coordinates.  The innovation \(U_i\) is used to generate a random four-cell schedule
\(V_i=(V_{i,00},V_{i,01},V_{i,10},V_{i,11})\in\{-b,b\}^4\), independently over \(i\).  Define
\[
 \mathcal H_0
 =\{v\in\{-b,b\}^4:v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}=0\}.
\]
This set has six elements.  Let \(Q_0\) be uniform on \(\mathcal H_0\).  Put
\[
 v^+=(-b,-b,b,b),\qquad v^-=-v^+,
\]
in the coordinate order \((00,01,10,11)\), let \(Q_1\) assign probability \(1/2\) to each of \(v^+\) and \(v^-\), and, for \(0\le t<1\), set
\[
 Q_t=(1-t)Q_0+tQ_1. \tag{2}
\]
A finite quantile partition of \([0,1]\) realizes each \(Q_t\) as a measurable function of \(U_i\).  Under the resulting law \(P_t\), define the common no-carryover schedule by
\[
 Y_i(d;U,G)=V_{i,C_i(d)}. \tag{3}
\]
The line is shift equivariant and has edge range one.  The exposure and outcome rules in (3) are shift equivariant and depend only on \((U_i,d_i,d_{i+1})\), so they are radius-one local and hence radius-\(r\) local because \(r\ge1\).  The outcome envelope follows from \(|V_{i,c}|=b\le B\).  Moreover
\(\pi_i(e_1)=\pi_i(e_0)=1/2\ge\varepsilon\), since the declared overlap constant satisfies \(\varepsilon<1/2\).  Together with the iid innovations and the two conditionally independent Bernoulli waves, these facts verify every condition defining \(P_t\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).

For a realized schedule \(V_i=v\), direct averaging over the four equiprobable local assignment cells gives
\[
 m_i
 =\mathbb E_{P_t}\!\left[
 Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=1)}{1/2}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=0)}{1/2}\right\}
 \middle|\mathcal F_U\right]
 =\frac{v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}}2. \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(m_i=0\) on \(\mathcal H_0\), whereas (4) equals \(a\) at \(v^+\) and \(-a\) at \(v^-\).  The symmetry of \(Q_t\) gives \(\tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i=0\).  Since the schedules are iid across sites, \((h_i)=(m_i)\) is iid, and hence
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i^2=a^2t,
 \qquad
 \gamma_h(k)=0\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_t)=a^2t. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, \(P_0\) is a null law and every \(P_t\), \(t>0\), is a positive alternative.  Equation (4) also proves that the parameter moved in (5) is the causal conditional exposure-effect score, rather than an arbitrary observed-law functional.

It remains to bound the information in the complete observation.  Condition on both assignment arrays.  At site \(i\), the two observed outcomes select the ordered cell pair \((c,c')=(C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)}))\).  Write \(R_j^{c,c'}\) for the law of \((V_{i,c},V_{i,c'})\) under \(Q_j\), \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and list atom probabilities in the order \((b,b),(b,-b),(-b,b),(-b,-b)\).  Exhaustive enumeration of the six schedules in \(\mathcal H_0\) and the two schedules \(v^+,v^-\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{ordered cell pair}&R_0^{c,c'}&R_1^{c,c'}\\ \hline
c=c'&(1/2,0,0,1/2)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\ne c'\text{ within }\{00,01\}\text{ or }\{10,11\}
 &(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\text{ and }c'\text{ in opposite exposure groups}
 &(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)&(0,1/2,1/2,0).
\end{array} \tag{6}
\]
The three rows cover all sixteen ordered pairs in \(\mathcal C^2\), so (6) is also the exact smallest-cell stress test.  In every row, each atom charged by \(R_1^{c,c'}\) has positive \(R_0^{c,c'}\)-probability.  Therefore the two-wave raw outcome law has common support even though the latent four-cell schedule law in (2) does not.

Let \(R_t^{c,c'}=(1-t)R_0^{c,c'}+tR_1^{c,c'}\).  For distinct cells, direct substitution from (6) yields
\[
 \sum_x\frac{\{R_1^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}=2, \tag{7}
\]
while the same quantity is zero when \(c=c'\).  Since \(\log u\le u-1\) for \(u>0\),
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{c,c'}\Vert R_0^{c,c'})
 \le \sum_x\frac{\{R_t^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}
 \le2t^2. \tag{8}
\]
Conditional on the assignments, the selected outcome pairs are independent over \(i\in I_n\), because the schedules \(V_i\) are independent.  The graph is the same deterministic line under \(P_t\) and \(P_0\); the assignments have the same law; and the exposures and propensity coordinates are deterministic functions of the graph and assignments.  Expanding the conditional product likelihood ratio, taking its logarithm, and then averaging first over the independent schedules and then over the common assignment law proves
\[
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(\mathcal L_{P_t}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \middle\Vert\mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 =\mathbb E_D\sum_{i\in I_n}
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}\Vert
 R_0^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})})
 \le2N_nt^2. \tag{9}
\]
Thus (9) is a chain-rule likelihood bound for the entire declared observation, not merely for its score coordinates.

Put \(\eta=1-\alpha-\beta>0\) and
\[
 t_0=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2N_n}}.
\]
Because \(0<\eta<1\) and \(N_n\ge1\), one has \(0<t_0<1\).  Pinsker's inequality and (9) give
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(\mathcal L_{P_{t_0}}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}),
 \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 \le\sqrt{N_nt_0^2}=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}. \tag{10}
\]
Let \(\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) be any randomized test satisfying
\(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\le\alpha\).  To use the binary form of the two-point testing lemma, adjoin under both laws a common independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and reject when \(A\le\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Integrating measurable sections shows that taking the product with this same uniform law leaves total variation unchanged.  The two-point lemma and (10) then imply
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{t_0}}[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}
 =\beta+\eta\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)>\beta. \tag{11}
\]
By (5),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_{t_0})
 =\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{12}
\]
For every candidate separation no larger than (12), the law \(P_{t_0}\) is in the corresponding alternative set and violates the required type-II bound in (11).  Taking the infimum in the definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) proves the lower bound.  Combining it with (1), choosing any fixed positive \(a\le2B\), using \(N_n=n-2r\), and using the established \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\) proves the asserted \(\Theta(n^{-1/2})\) rate.  The condition \(e_1\ne e_0\) is necessary: if the two labels coincide, the two terms in every exposure-IPW score cancel identically.

proposed.name: Canonical full-observable experiment and score subexperiment
proposed.construction:
For \(n>4r\), encode the complete finite observation as the single Euclidean vector
\[
 O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}
 =\Bigl(
   (\mathbf 1\{\{i,j\}\in G\})_{(i,j)\in\Lambda_n^2},
   (D_i^{(w)})_{i\in\Lambda_n,\,w\in\{1,2\}},
   (\mathbf 1\{E_i(D^{(w)},G)=e\})_{i\in I_n,\,w\in\{1,2\},\,e\in\mathcal E},
\]
\[
   (Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G))_{i\in I_n,\,w\in\{1,2\}},
   (\pi_i(e_0),\pi_i(e_1))_{i\in I_n}
 \Bigr)
 \in\mathbb R^{,n^2+2n+2N_n|\mathcal E|+4N_n}.
\]
The final propensity coordinates are known design quantities.  Thus the score vector
\[
 W_n=\bigl((Z_{n,i}^{(1)},Z_{n,i}^{(2)})\bigr)_{i\in I_n}
 \in\mathbb R^{2N_n}
\]
is a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\), by the displayed exposure-IPW formula and exposure positivity.  Let
\[
 \Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}
 =\{\varphi_n:\mathbb R^{,n^2+2n+2N_n|\mathcal E|+4N_n}\to[0,1]:
 \varphi_n\text{ is Borel measurable}\},
\]
and define
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 :=\inf\Bigl\{s\ge0:\ \exists\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\text{ such that }
 \mathbb E_P[\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]\le\alpha
 \text{ for every }P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\text{ with }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
\]
\[
 \hspace{45mm}
 \mathbb E_P[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]\le\beta
 \text{ for every }P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\text{ with }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge s\Bigr\}.
\]
The score subexperiment retains
\[
 \Psi_n=\{\psi_n:\mathbb R^{2N_n}\to[0,1]:\psi_n\text{ is Borel measurable}\}
\]
and
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{score}}
 :=\inf\Bigl\{s\ge0:\ \exists\psi_n\in\Psi_n\text{ such that }
 \mathbb E_P[\psi_n(W_n)]\le\alpha
 \text{ for every }P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\text{ with }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
\]
\[
 \hspace{45mm}
 \mathbb E_P[1-\psi_n(W_n)]\le\beta
 \text{ for every }P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\text{ with }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge s\Bigr\}.
\]
Both experiments use common, law-independent Borel maps.  The full vector contains the observed graph, both assignments, both exposures, and both realized outcomes; it does not reveal the innovations or unobserved assignment-cell outcomes.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorems 1--2 and Corollary 1 show that zero asymptotic variance for a stationary finite-variance finite-dependent sequence is equivalent to a finite-dependent coboundary and yields an unnormalized endpoint-difference law.
The paper proves consistency and asymptotic normality for exposure-IPW estimators under approximate neighborhood interference and studies network-HAC inference for one randomized finite population.
The paper proves central limit and invariance principles for stationary fields represented as functions of independent innovations under short-range physical dependence.
The paper proves treatment-effect asymptotics under graphon-random interference and develops direct- and indirect-effect inference.

The preprint proves asymptotic normality and optimality for regression-adjusted average-direct-effect estimators under graphon interference and consistently estimates the linear estimator's asymptotic variance under a low-rank graphon condition.

The preprint uses a first-wave pilot to estimate variance and optimizes second-wave participation and treatment assignments for average treatment and average spillover effects under network interference.

prose_updates.tldr: Two conditionally independent assignment waves on one no-carryover schedule identify the Palm population covariance through observable cross-wave IPW products. Bounded primitive influence, bounded score-dependency degree, a common Palm mean, and a fixed deterministic covariance-support pair set yield order-\(n^{-1}\) centering bias and root-\(n\) finite-sample concentration on F\o lner interiors, with the buffered integer interval giving the explicit size--power test and an exactly unbiased lag-separated version. A four-cell exact-local least-favorable schedule has common support for the entire observed graph--assignment--exposure--outcome vector and proves a matching full-observation minimax lower bound. Thus, for distinct focal exposure labels, both the full-observation and score-vector separation radii are \(\Theta(n^{-1/2})\) for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\), \(p=1/2\), and \(\alpha+\beta<1\).

project_justification.gap: Janson2015 classifies the zero-long-run-variance boundary for finite block factors, and the one-wave interference papers study effect or estimator-variance inference. Viviano2020 already develops a two-wave network design in which a pilot estimates variance and the second wave optimizes participation and treatment; none of these works supplies a repeated-randomization test of the Palm population-covariance boundary or a full-observation minimax converse for it.
project_justification.niche: Conditional replication removes assignment noise from cross-wave IPW products. Fixed local dependency sets make the quadratic diagnostic concentrate on deterministic F\o lner interiors, while four local assignment cells leave unobserved schedule coordinates after two waves and permit a common-support full-data information bound.
project_justification.fill: The project gives the cross-wave identity, order-\(n^{-1}\) centering control, root-\(n\) concentration, finite-sample size and power, and an exactly unbiased lag-separated interval statistic. For distinct focal exposure labels, it also constructs a causal-realizable four-cell submodel with \(\operatorname{KL}\le2N_ns^2\) and linearly changing \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\), proving matching \(\Theta(n^{-1/2})\) minimax rates for the complete declared observation and, as a corollary, for the score vector.

sampling_model.design: Two conditionally independent Bernoulli assignment waves with known probability \(p\) are applied to the same graph, exposure mapping, and no-carryover potential-outcome schedule after a prespecified washout; the deterministic covariance cutoff and analysis interior are fixed before assignment.
sampling_model.units: The canonical specialization observes \(\Lambda_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and analyzes its buffered interior \(I_n\). The dependency-set formulation also covers deterministic F\o lner interiors of bounded-degree vertex-transitive amenable graphs, including amenable Cayley graphs, under fixed local range.
sampling_model.treatment: Binary assignments in each wave generate local exposure labels and realized outcomes under one common schedule; the full minimax observation contains the finite graph, both assignments, both exposure arrays, both realized-outcome arrays, and known propensity coordinates.
sampling_model.overlap: Both focal exposures have conditional probability at least \(\varepsilon\) in each wave, so every IPW division is well defined.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Propensities are known from the design. The mean-centered statistic estimates only the two wave means, the lag-separated statistic removes that centering bias exactly, and neither procedure estimates unit-specific conditional scores or fits a regression.

prose_updates.related_work: Janson2015 supplies the finite-dependent coboundary result used to interpret the zero boundary, but no two-wave statistic or testing experiment. Leung2022ANI supplies one-wave exposure-IPW and approximate-neighborhood-interference analysis; no ANI or graph-HAC transfer is used here. AronowSamii2017 supplies exposure mappings and known design propensities. Viviano2020 is the closest design comparator: it uses a first-wave pilot to estimate variance and optimizes second-wave participation and treatment for average treatment and spillover effects. The present work does not claim that two-wave network designs are new; it instead uses conditionally independent replications to identify and test a Palm covariance boundary and proves a full-observation common-support minimax converse. LiWager2022 and FanLengWu2025 target causal-effect estimation and estimator variance under graphon models. Tsybakov2009 supplies the classical Pinsker and two-point testing inequalities used after the new four-cell likelihood calculation.
prose_updates.interpretation: The null \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\) is a covariance-cancellation boundary, not a claim that conditional exposure effects are homogeneous. On the line, Janson's result represents the null score as a finite-block coboundary. Rejection certifies positive Palm population variation; failure to reject only places that variation within the stated finite-sample threshold.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The design requires two conditionally independent assignment waves applied to one no-carryover schedule. The full-observation converse includes the observed finite graph, assignments, exposures, realized outcomes, and known propensities, but not the innovations or unobserved assignment-cell outcomes. The graph extension requires deterministic fixed-range dependency and covariance-support sets on F\o lner interiors. No growing bandwidth, random shortest-path cutoff, approximate-neighborhood-interference transfer, endogenous graph-distance HAC, annealed CLT or Wald theorem, or BondEtAl2012 reanalysis is claimed.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The causal target is \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\), the long-run covariance sum of fixed local conditional exposure-effect scores under the Palm law. The interval results and their bounded-degree vertex-transitive amenable-graph extension use a fixed deterministic local cutoff, bounded outcomes, overlap, two conditionally independent waves, bounded primitive influence, bounded score dependency, and a common Palm mean. For distinct focal exposure labels, minimax sharpness holds for the explicitly encoded finite observed-data vector at \(p=1/2\) and \(\alpha+\beta<1\); the score-vector theorem is a corollary. The note claims neither novelty of two-wave designs nor validity for richer observations that reveal innovations or unobserved potential outcomes.

statement_notes.justification: This theorem certifies root-sample-size optimality even when a test uses the complete declared experimental record rather than only precomputed scores.
statement_notes.gap: Viviano2020 studies pilot-based second-wave design optimization, not a common-support information lower bound for testing the Palm covariance boundary.
statement_notes.consumer: A designer can use the finite-sample upper threshold knowing that no common Borel test of the declared full observation improves its separation order uniformly over the class.

statement_notes.justification: The score-vector result is retained as an operational corollary of the stronger full-observable minimax theorem.
statement_notes.gap: The earlier four-atom score construction did not survive observation of raw outcomes; the new four-cell schedule closes the full-data likelihood comparison before restriction to scores.
statement_notes.consumer: Implementations that retain only the two IPW score arrays inherit the same sharp root-sample-size separation rate.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), \(n>4r\), \(i\in I_n\), and
\(w\in\{1,2\}\).  Couple the finite-volume wave to the restriction
\(D^{(w)}|_{\Lambda_n}\) of the infinite assignment field, as prescribed by the
buffered-restriction definition.  Since \(i\in I_n\),
\[
 \{i-r,\ldots,i+r\}\subseteq\Lambda_n. \tag{1}
\]
The score-locality assumption says that the exposure and realized potential
outcome entering \(Z_i^{(w)}\) are measurable functions only of
\((U_j,D_j^{(w)})\) for the indices in (1).  The graph edge-range assumption
ensures that restricting the graph to \(\Lambda_n\) removes no neighbor of
\(i\).  Thus the local exposure and outcome in the finite and infinite
constructions agree under this coupling.  Moreover, conditional on
\(\mathcal F_U\), both constructions use the same product
\(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) law on the coordinates in (1).  Hence their
conditional exposure probabilities agree.  Exposure positivity makes both
denominators in the IPW score at least \(\varepsilon>0\), so division is valid
and every factor in the two score formulas agrees.  Therefore
\[
 Z_{n,i}^{(w)}=Z_i^{(w)}\qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{2}
\]

Finally, \(\Lambda_n\setminus I_n\) consists of exactly the \(r\) left-end
sites and the \(r\) right-end sites.  Since \(|\Lambda_n|=n\) and \(r\) is
fixed,
\[
 \frac{|\Lambda_n\setminus I_n|}{|\Lambda_n|}
 =\frac{2r}{n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This proves both assertions.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) and \(i,j\in\mathbb Z\).  The
score-envelope part of the exact score-split lemma gives
\(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K\), so all conditional expectations and products below are
integrable.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), the graph, exposure maps, and
common no-carryover potential-outcome schedule are fixed.  Each
\(Z_i^{(w)}\) is then a measurable function of the assignment field
\(D^{(w)}\).  The cross-wave-independence assumption therefore implies
conditional independence of \(Z_i^{(1)}\) and \(Z_j^{(2)}\), even when their
within-wave assignment neighborhoods overlap.  Since the two waves have the
same conditional Bernoulli design, the definition of \(m_i\) and conditional
independence yield
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
  \mathbb E_P[Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =m_i m_j. \tag{1}
\]

The iid-innovation assumption together with graph, exposure, and outcome
equivariance makes \((m_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) stationary.  Consequently
\(\mathbb E_Pm_i=\mathbb E_Pm_0=\tau_{\mathrm P}\), and the definition
\(h_i=m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P}\) gives \(\mathbb E_Ph_i=0\).  Taking expectations
in (1), setting \(i=0\) and \(j=k\), and using
\(m_i=\tau_{\mathrm P}+h_i\), we obtain
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[m_0m_k]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[h_0h_k]
 =\gamma_h(k). \tag{2}
\]
By definition, the causal Palm population variance is
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)\).  Summing (2) over
this fixed covariance-support set proves
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}
   \{\mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2\}.
\]
Thus the observed-law cross-wave moment identifies the already-defined causal
functional; the equality is not being imposed as a definition.

Fix \(n>4r\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and
\(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Apply the fixed-footprint Cayley/F\o lner
concentration theorem to the additive group \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\) with
\[
 A=\{-r,\ldots,r\},\qquad
 C=A-A=\{-2r,\ldots,2r\}.
\]
Then \(a=|A|=2r+1\), \(q=|C|=4r+1\), \(\Lambda=\Lambda_n\), and the theorem's
interior \(I\) equals \(I_n\).  Its pair sets are exactly \(J_{n,k}\), and
\[
 N=N_n=n-2r,\qquad
 \nu=\min_{|k|\le2r}N_{n,k}=n-4r>0,\qquad
 |\Lambda|=n. \tag{1}
\]

We verify every primitive premise of that theorem.  By score locality, the
score at \(i\) depends only on
\((U_j,D_j^{(w)})_{i-r\le j\le i+r}\), so a primitive coordinate influences
at most \(2r+1\) scores in its wave.  Exposure and outcome equivariance give
the common translation-equivariant score rule.  The exact score-split lemma
and exposure positivity give \(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K=B/\varepsilon<\infty\).
The wavewise Bernoulli assumption says that the conditional law of each wave
is the fixed product Bernoulli law, independent of the value of \(U\), and
cross-wave independence factors the two conditional wave laws.  Writing
\(\mu_p\) for that product law, for cylinder events \(A_U,B_1,B_2\) we have
\[
 P\{U\in A_U,D^{(1)}\in B_1,D^{(2)}\in B_2\}
 =P(U\in A_U)\,\mu_p(B_1)\,\mu_p(B_2), \tag{2}
\]
so the iid innovation coordinates and both assignment-coordinate families
are mutually independent.  The buffered-coupling proposition identifies the
finite scores used by \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\) with these local infinite
scores on \(I_n\).  Finally, the cross-wave-identification lemma identifies
the theorem's \(\Omega\) with the already-defined causal functional
\(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\).

The generic bias allowance specialized through (1) is
\[
 \frac{4q^2K^2}{N}
 =\frac{4(4r+1)^2K^2}{N_n}=b_n, \tag{3}
\]
and its deviation allowance is
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,a qK^2}{\nu}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =\frac{\sqrt{48n}(2r+1)(4r+1)K^2}{n-4r}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =q_n(\delta). \tag{4}
\]
Equations (3)--(4) and the theorem therefore give
\[
 P\{|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|
       >b_n+q_n(\delta)\}\le\delta. \tag{5}
\]
The right side and both allowances depend on the model law only through the
common constants \(r\), \(B\), and \(\varepsilon\).  Taking the supremum of
(5) over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) proves the stated uniform bound.

As the prescribed smallest-instance check, take \(r=1\), \(n=5\), the
deterministic line graph, \(E_i(d)=d_i\), \(p=1/2\), and the bounded schedule
\(Y_i(d)=Bd_i\).  Then \(N_n=3\), \(Z_i^{(w)}=2BD_i^{(w)}\),
\(m_i=B\), \(h_i=0\), and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\).  For each of the
\(2^{10}\) possible two-wave assignment vectors, every lag-product average
and the product of the two wave means lies in \([0,4B^2]\), whence
\(|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}|\le20B^2\).  Because
\(K=B/\varepsilon>2B\),
\[
 b_n=\frac{4\cdot25K^2}{3}>\frac{400B^2}{3}>20B^2.
\]
Thus no assignment rejects, and averaging the same exhaustive collection of
assignments gives \(\mathbb E_P\widehat\Omega_n^{12}=0\).  This check is
consistent with both the exact bias identity and the asserted size bound.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\Gamma\) be a countable finitely generated group with identity \(e\),
equipped with a finite symmetric generating set and hence with its
bounded-degree vertex-transitive Cayley graph.  Fix a finite set
\(A\subset\Gamma\) with \(e\in A\), and declare the finite covariance-support
set \(C=AA^{-1}\), with \(a=|A|\) and \(q=|C|\).  Let
\(\Lambda\subset\Gamma\) be finite, put
\[
 I=\{v\in\Lambda:vA\subseteq\Lambda\},\qquad
 J_g=\{v\in I:vg\in I\},\qquad
 N=|I|,\qquad \nu=\min_{g\in C}|J_g|,
\]
and suppose \(N>0\) and \(\nu>0\).  Let \((U_v)_{v\in\Gamma}\) be iid.
Conditional on \(\sigma(U)\), let \(D^{(1)}\) and \(D^{(2)}\) be independent,
with the coordinates within each wave iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_0)\)
for a fixed \(p_0\in(0,1)\).  Fix two exposure labels \(c_1,c_0\), a
no-carryover, \(\Gamma\)-equivariant exposure map \(E_v\), and a common
potential-outcome schedule \(Y_v\).  For the known positive propensities
\[
 \pi_v(c)=\Pr\{E_v(D^{(w)})=c\mid\sigma(U)\}>0,
\]
define the exposure-IPW scores explicitly by
\[
 Z_v^{(w)}=Y_v(D^{(w)};U)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(E_v(D^{(w)})=c_1)}{\pi_v(c_1)}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(E_v(D^{(w)})=c_0)}{\pi_v(c_0)}\right\}.
\]
Suppose that these scores satisfy: (i) the same measurable score rule is used
in both waves; (ii)
\(Z_v^{(w)}\) depends only on \((U_{vx},D_{vx}^{(w)})_{x\in A}\); and (iii)
\(|Z_v^{(w)}|\le K_0\) almost surely for a fixed \(K_0<\infty\).
Define
\[
 m_v=\mathbb E[Z_v^{(w)}\mid\sigma(U)],\quad
 \tau=\mathbb E[m_e],\quad h_v=m_v-\tau,\quad
 \gamma(g)=\mathbb E[h_eh_g],\quad
 \Omega=\sum_{g\in C}\gamma(g),
\]
and, under the common restriction coupling, define
\[
 \overline Z^{(w)}=\frac1N\sum_{v\in I}Z_v^{(w)},\qquad
 \widehat\Omega
 =\sum_{g\in C}\left\{
   \frac1{|J_g|}\sum_{v\in J_g}Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}
   -\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)}\right\}.
\]
Then, for every \(g\in C\),
\[
 \mathbb E[Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}\mid\sigma(U)]=m_vm_{vg},
\]
and
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat\Omega]
 =\Omega-q\operatorname{Var}\!\left(N^{-1}\sum_{v\in I}m_v\right),
 \qquad
 0\le \Omega-\mathbb E[\widehat\Omega]
 \le \frac{4q^2K_0^2}{N}. \tag{1}
\]
For every \(\delta\in(0,1)\),
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{
  |\widehat\Omega-\Omega|>
  \frac{4q^2K_0^2}{N}
  +\frac{\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,a qK_0^2}{\nu}
    \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 \right\}\le\delta. \tag{2}
\]
If \((\Lambda_j)\) is a right F\o lner sequence, meaning
\(|\Lambda_j\mathbin\triangle\Lambda_jg|/|\Lambda_j|\to0\) for every fixed
\(g\in\Gamma\), and \(A\), hence \(C\), is fixed, then
\(N_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\), \(\nu_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\), the bias in (1) is
\(O(|\Lambda_j|^{-1})\), and the deviation radius in (2) is
\(O(\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/|\Lambda_j|})\).  Thus the fixed-cutoff Palm
population-variance diagnostic has root-volume concentration on every such
amenable Cayley graph; no growing bandwidth or random graph distance is used.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
First note that the conditional assignment distribution is fixed and does not
depend on \(U\).  Write \(\mu_{p_0}\) for the product Bernoulli law with
success probability \(p_0\).  For cylinder events \(A_U,B_1,B_2\), conditional
wave independence and the two fixed product Bernoulli laws give
\[
 \Pr\{U\in A_U,D^{(1)}\in B_1,D^{(2)}\in B_2\}
 =\Pr(U\in A_U)\,\mu_{p_0}(B_1)\,\mu_{p_0}(B_2). \tag{3}
\]
Hence all environment coordinates and all assignment coordinates in the two
waves are mutually independent.  Integrating the local score rule over the
fixed assignment law also shows that \(m_v\) is a measurable function only of
\((U_{vx})_{x\in A}\).  Equivariance and the iid law make \((m_v)\) stationary,
so \(\mathbb E m_v=\tau\).  If \(u=vg\) and \(vA\cap uA\ne\varnothing\), then
there are \(x,y\in A\) with \(vx=vgy\), whence \(g=xy^{-1}\in AA^{-1}=C\).
It follows by independence of disjoint innovation blocks that
\[
 \mathbb E[h_vh_{vg}]=0\qquad(g\notin C). \tag{4}
\]
This derives the declared covariance support from the primitive footprint
condition; it is not an asymptotic-normality assumption.

Given \(\sigma(U)\), a score from wave one and a score from wave two are
functions of conditionally independent assignment fields.  The common score
rule therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb E[Z_v^{(1)}Z_u^{(2)}\mid\sigma(U)]=m_vm_u. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, stationarity and (5) imply, for \(g\in C\),
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[|J_g|^{-1}\sum_{v\in J_g}
 Z_v^{(1)}Z_{vg}^{(2)}\right]
 =\tau^2+\gamma(g). \tag{6}
\]
Conditional independence of the two entire waves also yields, with
\(\overline m=N^{-1}\sum_{v\in I}m_v\),
\[
 \mathbb E[\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)}]
 =\mathbb E[\overline m^{,2}]
 =\tau^2+\operatorname{Var}(\overline m). \tag{7}
\]
Subtracting \(q\) copies of (7) from the sum of (6) proves the expectation
identity in (1).  Since \(|m_v|\le K_0\) and \(|\tau|\le K_0\), one has
\(|h_v|\le2K_0\).  By (4), for each \(v\) at most \(q\) indices \(u\) can
have nonzero covariance with \(h_v\).  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\overline m)
 =\frac1{N^2}\sum_{u,v\in I}\mathbb E[h_uh_v]
 \le\frac{4qK_0^2}{N}. \tag{8}
\]
Multiplication by \(q\) establishes both inequalities in (1).

It remains to prove concentration from bounded primitive influence.  Because
each score is essentially bounded by \(K_0\), replacing it on its null
exceptional set by its clipping to \([-K_0,K_0]\) does not change any displayed
law or expectation and supplies an everywhere-bounded local version.  Write
\(T\) for the sum of the \(q\) lagged product averages and
\(R=q\overline Z^{(1)}\overline Z^{(2)}\), so that
\(\widehat\Omega=T-R\).  A single environment coordinate \(U_x\) can affect
at most \(a\) scores in each wave.  At a fixed \(g\), it can therefore affect
at most \(2a\) products.  Since every product lies in
\([-K_0^2,K_0^2]\), changing \(U_x\) changes \(T\) by at most
\(4aqK_0^2/\nu\).  Each wave mean changes by at most \(2aK_0/N\), while both
means remain in \([-K_0,K_0]\); hence \(R\) changes by at most
\(4aqK_0^2/N\le4aqK_0^2/\nu\).  Thus the oscillation caused by one environment
coordinate is at most
\[
 8c,\qquad c=\frac{aqK_0^2}{\nu}. \tag{9}
\]
A coordinate in only one assignment wave affects at most \(a\) products per
lag and only one sample mean.  The corresponding bounds are
\(2aqK_0^2/\nu\) for \(T\) and \(2aqK_0^2/N\) for \(R\), so its total
oscillation is at most \(4c\).

All scores retained in \(I\) use primitive coordinates in
\(IA\subseteq\Lambda\).  We may therefore view \(\widehat\Omega\) as a
function of at most \(|\Lambda|\) environment coordinates and at most
\(|\Lambda|\) assignment coordinates in each wave.  Enlarging the coordinate
list by unused independent coordinates does not change the statistic, and
the sum of squared oscillation bounds is at most
\[
 |\Lambda|(8c)^2+2|\Lambda|(4c)^2=96|\Lambda|c^2. \tag{10}
\]
McDiarmid's bounded-differences lemma, first with every bound in (9)--(10)
multiplied by \(1+\eta\) and then with \(\eta\downarrow0\), gives, for \(t>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{|\widehat\Omega-\mathbb E\widehat\Omega|>t\}
 \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2}{48|\Lambda|c^2}\right\}. \tag{11}
\]
At
\(t=\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,c\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}\), (11), (1), and the
triangle inequality prove (2).

Finally suppose \((\Lambda_j)\) is right F\o lner.  Since \(A\) is finite,
the union bound gives
\[
 \frac{|\Lambda_j\setminus I_j|}{|\Lambda_j|}
 \le\sum_{x\in A}
 \frac{|\Lambda_j\setminus\Lambda_jx^{-1}|}{|\Lambda_j|}
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{12}
\]
Thus \(N_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  For each fixed \(g\in C\), the same argument,
applied to \(I_j\setminus(I_jg^{-1})\) and using (12), gives
\(|J_{j,g}|/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  Finiteness of \(C\) permits taking the
minimum, so \(\nu_j/|\Lambda_j|\to1\).  Substitution in (1)--(2) yields the
two asserted rates and completes the proof.

proposed.name: Two-wave finite-range Palm exposure class
proposed.construction: \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}:=\{P:(U_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\text{ is iid};\ G\text{ is shift equivariant and every neighbor of }i\text{ lies in }\{i-r,\ldots,i+r\}\text{ for every }i;\ E_i\text{ and }Y_i\text{ are shift equivariant and radius-}r\text{ score local};\ |Y_i(d;U,G)|\le B;\ D^{(1)}\text{ and }D^{(2)}\text{ are conditionally independent given }\mathcal F_U;\ D_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U\text{ are iid }\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p);\ \min_{a\in\{e_1,e_0\}}\pi_i(a)\ge\varepsilon\text{ for every }i\in\mathbb Z\}\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The graph-rule-locality condition is not used by the score coupling, identification, bias, or concentration arguments. The operative primitives are score locality and graph edge range, so the class must state exactly those surviving conditions before the obsolete assumption is deleted.
After replacing the class definition, no live node needs graph-rule locality; score locality controls primitive influence and graph edge range controls the buffered restriction.

proposed.justification: The explicit uniform deviation inequality is the load-bearing result that turns the latent Janson boundary into a finite-sample observable object.
proposed.gap: Janson2015 classifies zero long-run variance but supplies no test from randomized causal scores; FanLengWu2025 estimates the asymptotic variance of a regression-adjusted direct-effect estimator under a low-rank graphon model and does not give this two-wave finite-sample bound.
proposed.consumer: Repeated online experiments obtain a prespecified, regression-free error bar for the population component even when the null lies on a degenerate coboundary boundary.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof now specializes the explicit bounded-influence and dependency-set theorem on fixed-footprint amenable Cayley graphs, so that theorem must be declared as a direct dependency.
